Hayley was under the NHS mental health services for over 30 years, given nine different psychiatric diagnoses, prescribed 28 different psychiatric medications and had countless hospital admissions. 

When she was eventually diagnosed as having a hormone imbalance and prescribed bioidentical estradiol, progesterone and testosterone, her quality of life improved and is now the most well both physically and mentally she has been for decades. 

Her son Jay shared her story on my tour this summer which resonated with so many people. 

Hayley has recently moved to a different area and her new GP practice has just refused to prescribe any hormone treatments to her as they are concerned about the dose of hormone treatments she is prescribed, despite no evidence of harm. They have told her than is she receives care and treatment from my clinic then they will not prescribe any doses of hormone treatments to her. This is despite acknowledging how much she has improved. This is not acceptable. 

She is still being prescribed psychiatric medications by her GP and those are associated with both risks and side effects. Saying no to hormone treatments for her is associated with risks too, including a risk to her mental health deteriorating.

Please share this post with anyone who needs to see what is happening to women like Hayley. So much really needs to change.

Why are only around 5% of menopausal women prescribed HRT?

This week on my drlouisenewsonpodcast, Dr Jerrold Weinberg menopausemended, an obstetrician and gynaecologist who has practised medicine for 50 years, explained how we got here. When a woman stops making estradiol, the simple answer is to replace it, yet there are still unfounded fears about HRT. The first hormone treatments were made from pregnant mares' urine (Premarin) and the synthetic progestogen medroxyprogesterone acetate (Provera) which are associated with small risks. However, these are very different to the bioidentical hormone treatments we prescribe now which are not associated with these risks. However, there are a whole generation of doctors who have not been trained to prescribe hormone treatments.

The bioidentical hormone treatments, progesterone, estradiol and testosterone, which we prescribe now are the same structure as the hormones our bodies make and are therefore very different from the older types of HRT. Women who are prescribed the right dose and type of bioidentical hormone treatments often them feel like themselves again, as well as having better future health.

Every woman struggling with symptoms of hormonal changes, at any age, deserves the chance to make an informed choice about being prescribed hormone treatments.

If you're a healthcare professional, or you know one who needs to hear this, please encourage them to do our newson.education course. Listen to the full conversation now via the link in my bio.

Hormone treatments are often considered as the “risky” option yet bioidentical hormones treatments are far safer than so many medications we prescribe. 

For my daughter Jess, hormone treatments were the only treatments that didn't cause dreadful side effects and have improved her quality of life. 

Over around seven years she has been prescribed a long list of medications for migraine, many were prescribed off license and these were seen as the safe, standard choices. 

She had side effects including dry mouth, blurred vision, low mood, dizziness and memory loss with various medications. Horrendous to witness and awful for her to experience. 

Bioidentical progesterone, estradiol and testosterone have the same structure as the hormones our bodies make, so they work very differently to synthetic hormones in contraceptives and older types of HRT. 

For many women and girls whose migraines or mood are caused by hormone changes, they can be one of the most effective treatments available. 

Every woman deserves accurate information about different treatments, including bioidentical hormone treatments for younger women. 

If you know someone who has been told hormones are too “risky” to consider, please share this post with them.

“Too young”, “too old”, “too risky” to be prescribed hormone treatments…

These are just some of the things women are told when seeking help for their hormone health.

So many women are being refused hormone treatments - progesterone, estradiol and testosterone - which they both need and want. 

Many women are still being wrongly told their symptoms are “normal”, that they’re imagining them or that hormone treatments are too “dangerous”. Often without a proper discussion about the evidence or their individual circumstances.

For my Halloween live Q&A on my YouTube, I asked you to share some of the frightening things you’ve been told about your hormones so I could separate fact from fiction. 

I’ve shared five of the many questions I responded to here, and there are many more which you can watch on my YouTube channel, Dr Louise Newson. Link in bio.

I’d love to know, what’s the most frightening thing you’ve ever been told about your hormones or hormone treatments?

Which is safer to prescribe to a menopausal woman with osteoporosis, a bisphosphonate or HRT?

I saw a woman in my newson.health clinic who is 62 and has been without hormones for 20 years, since her periods stopped at 42. No one considered hormone treatments then and she was told the risks were too high. Now she doesn’t want to take bisphosphonates because she’s read about their risks, yet she’s been told she has to. 

Her GP documented what he thought the risks of HRT are, including cardiovascular disease, stroke and breast cancer, but not that those risks relate to synthetic hormones rather than the body identical hormones we prescribe now. She was also offered an antidepressant for slightly low mood, even though SSRIs are associated with lower bone density, and she’s already worried about another fracture.

Estradiol, progesterone and testosterone work physiologically on bone, helping osteoblasts build it and reducing the osteoclasts that break it down. Women deserve a choice and the best evidence. It is not right to withhold hormone treatments - progesterone, estradiol and testosterone - when that is what they both need and want.

So many women have a hormone imbalance and far too many women are being dismissed.

When I was a junior doctor I never heard women saying they weren’t listened to or believed, yet now I hear it every day in my newson.health clinic and on social media. I listened to this guardianscience  podcast today about perimenopause. 

Of course it is great that more women are talking about perimenopause but it is important that both clincians and women understand the hormonal imbalances that occur and the best ways of treating them. 

There was discussion here that many women’s symptoms could be due to “stress” and women were encouraged to change their lifestyle to improve symptoms such as increase exercise. 

They also spoke about women being prescribed “hormonal” contraception and wait until they are 50 before considering taking HRT. 

Hormone levels start to fluctuate and fall long before menopause, and those changes affect the brain, bones, heart and every other system in the body, causing many symptoms including mood changes and anxiety - important to consider rather than giving women the label of “stress”. 

We should also have healthy lifestyles but they won’t replace hormones that are low.

Contraception contains synthetic hormones, which actually can block the action of your own hormones (progesterone, estradiol and testosterone) and are associated with risks of clot, heart disease, stroke and cancers, unlike bioidentical hormone treatments. 

If the underlying cause of a woman’s symptoms is low hormones, we should be replacing them with the right dose and type of hormone treatment. 

Every woman deserves accurate information so she can make her own choice about taking hormone treatments. 

Women deserve to feel better and live healthier lives by having better access to bioidentical hormone treatments - progesterone, estradiol and testosterone - and also to vaginal hormones.

Does menopause speed up ageing and can estrogen slow it down?

nikolinalauc, CEO of glycanage, joined me on my drlouisenewsonpodcast to explain what her research shows about inflammation, ageing and the menopause transition.

Before menopause, women are in a way protected against low-grade inflammation, and when you compare their immune systems with men's, they look much younger. Nikolina's research with Professor Tim Spector found that from perimenopause to menopause, this marker of immune ageing changes twice as fast as at any other time in a woman's life, which helps explain why heart disease and diabetes so often appear after menopause. Studies have shown that estrogen can prevent this acceleration, and in a group of women from my newson.health clinic, inflammation fell with HRT.

When a recent review of UK Biobank data identified 14 drugs with the potential to extend life, four of them were estrogens, and yet the longevity world is focused on new drugs because estrogen is generic. Many diseases of ageing are inflammatory, and while we can't always prevent them, we may be able to delay them, so women can stay healthier for longer.

Progesterone is such an important hormone for women, yet there is still so much confusion about the different types, doses and ways it can be taken.

I often hear from women who have been told they are ‘progesterone intolerant’ because they’ve experienced unwanted symptoms while taking it. However, this doesn’t always mean progesterone itself is the problem - it’s more commonly an intolerance to synthetic progestogens or some of the preservatives in the progesterone. 

The type of hormone, dose and method of administration can all make a difference too. Understanding these options is so important when finding the right treatment for each individual woman.

In my latest live Q&A, I answered your questions about progesterone, including how to manage unwanted symptoms, the differences between preparations and why individualised treatment matters.

Every day I hear from women who've been told they don't need HRT, that antidepressants will help instead or that their GP can't prescribe testosterone.

Recently I’ve been speaking to the founder of HRTlottery which is free online tool that lets women check their GP surgery’s record on hormone treatment (HRT) and testosterone prescribing and see how it compares to other surgeries nearby.

What we have seen when looking into this data is that women in some parts of England are prescribed more than five times as much HRT as women in others. In the wealthiest areas, 1 in 4 women are on HRT. In the poorest, it's 1 in 10.

That isn't good medicine. It's luck!

And if HRT is a lottery, testosterone is even worse. Women need testosterone for their mood, energy, concentration and sex drive. Yet in most areas your GP isn't allowed to start it, and the only testosterone licensed for women in the UK is private-only. Far too many women go without it, or end up paying for it themselves.

This is not about blaming GPs. Most GPs haven’t been taught about hormone health and are working in systems that don’t allow then to prescribe. 

But we need to be looking at this data and we can’t ignore what we’ve seen. Until every doctor gets proper hormone health education, women will keep paying for it with their health and it’s not good enough. 

So it’s worth using HRTlottery, seeing how your GP practice stands up against others and if they are falling behind, share our newson_education programme with them so they can become confident in prescribing hormone treatments.

Families affected by Primodos have waited decades for justice, and today the Prime Minister, andy.burnham, announced his support for them.

For those that don’t know, Primodos was a hormone pregnancy test prescribed to millions of women in the UK between 1958 and 1978, and it had never been tested in pregnancy. 

It contained ethinylestradiol and norethisterone, two synthetic hormones that are still prescribed every day to millions of women for contraception and also to delay periods.

Tomorrow, Marie Lyon joins me on my drlouisenewsonpodcast. Marie was prescribed Primodos by her GP in 1970, and she has spent decades campaigning for answers as chair of the Association for Children Damaged by Hormone Pregnancy Tests. Babies of women who took Primodos when they were pregnant were born with many different congenital abnormalities including cleft lip, cleft palate, heart defects, spina bifida, and limb abnormalities.

The safety of contraceptive hormones in pregnancy has never been properly tested. 

The decision was made by the Committee of Safety of Medicine not to put out a public warning about it because they were worried that women would be scared about the contraceptive Pill. Instead, the went to Schering, the drug company, to warn them about this. 

This is why I think tomorrow’s episode is so important for everyone to listen to. The families affected are still living with the harm and still waiting for answers, and even now women can only make a true choice about what they put in their body when they know the full story.

Testosterone is the most biologically active hormone a woman has, and we have testosterone receptors in every cell of our body. It affects our brain, bones, muscles and immune system, and our levels start to fall from our late 20s and early 30s.

So when doctors in the media say testosterone prescribing is “out of control”, I disagree. Only around 0.82% of women who may benefit from testosterone in the UK are prescribed it. That’s nowhere near as out of control as antidepressant prescribing, and many women I see are on antidepressants, painkillers or sleeping tablets for symptoms of low testosterone and so what they really need is treatment with testosterone.

Also describing testosterone prescribing as being “abusive” makes no sense to me either!

At my newson.health clinic over 44,000 women have been prescribed testosterone in the past 8 years. In our research, women who were still struggling on HRT reported improvements in many symptoms including in mood and cognition after using testosterone. 

Reassuringly, the incidence of side effects is very low indeed in our patients who are using testosterone. Testosterone is also about so much more than libido.

Estradiol, progesterone and testosterone all have different roles in our bodies, so we need to think about each hormone  separately. 

Women who want and need testosterone should be able to get it prescribed for them.

Today is World Menopause Day. So let’s ask the uncomfortable question: what has actually changed for women since last year?

Sadly, the honest answer is when it comes to women’s hormone health, so much is going backwards.

The proportion of women prescribed HRT is now at its lowest level since 2002. Testosterone is prescribed to less than 1% of women in England who could benefit from it. HRT prescribing is consistently lower in areas of deprivation. Some Estradot patches have been in short supply since December 2024, and that’s now expected to run into 2027.

Every day, my colleagues and I from my newson.health clinic, my balancehormonehealth app and around the world hear from women who have done everything right. They’ve read the evidence, tracked their symptoms and asked for help, only to be incorrectly told they’re too young, too old or their blood tests are “normal”. Too many are handed an antidepressant and a leaflet about mindfulness instead.

Meanwhile, a menowashing industry has rushed to fill the gap with supplements, teas, cooling pillows and even chocolate bars. None of them can replace the hormones a woman’s body is lacking.

So here’s my challenge this World Menopause Day: let’s stop talking about menopause, and start talking about hormones. Progesterone, estradiol and testosterone work on every cell in our bodies, and hormone imbalances can affect women at every age, not just one moment in time.

Women need to have easier access to hormone treatments. 

Women’s hormones don’t take 364 days off. This needs to be a conversation all year round. What will be different for women by this time next year?

Read the full piece I’ve written with jill.chmielewski and pollard70 on our new Substack, The Third Opinion. I’ll share a link in my story now.

Women deserve better hormone healthcare, and that starts with education. It is shocking that doctors can qualify with as little as one hour of menopause education during their entire medical training.

Hormone imbalances also occur in women with PMS, PMDD, endometriosis, PCOS, ADHD, Ehlers Danlos syndrome, PoTS, MCAS, histamine intolerance, migraines, postnatal depression, postnatal psychosis and perimenopause.

Yet so many women are misdiagnosed with fibromyalgia, depression, personality disorders, bipolar disorder or chronic fatigue syndrome without a hormonal imbalance being considered. And many doctors around the world still refuse to prescribe hormone treatments (HRT), which improve both symptoms and future health.

Yesterday, I joined our newson_education and balancehormonehealth app teams at the loveandpowerorg menopause and hormone health campaign event, supporting their call for every GP surgery in the UK to have at least one healthcare professional trained in menopause and women’s hormone health.

But it’s not just GPs. Psychiatrists, cardiologists, urologists, gastroenterologists, neurologists and other specialists all need to understand hormonal imbalances and how to treat them.

Women should not have to fight to be listened to, struggle to access hormone treatments or pay privately because their healthcare professionals haven’t been adequately trained. Too many women are being harmed by a lack of understanding of hormones and safe prescribing of progesterone, estradiol and testosterone. This needs to change, and fast.

Please share our newson_education courses with your doctor. Our evidence-based course gives healthcare professionals the knowledge and confidence to recognise symptoms and prescribe appropriate hormone treatments.

If you’re a healthcare professional, please take the time to improve your knowledge. It could transform the lives of so many women.

Many women with endometriosis are told they can't take HRT, and that simply isn't true.

This week on my drlouisenewsonpodcast, Nicola Roberts joined me to share her experience of living with endometriosis since her periods started at the age of 12. She was put on the pill at 13 and diagnosed with stage 4 endometriosis at 25, and she then spent years on the Depo-Provera injection, which left her with low mood, body aches and osteoporosis by the age of 40.

Depo-Provera contains a synthetic progestogen that works by blocking the action of estradiol in the body and the brain, so it's a bit like giving someone a menopause straight off. Many of the women I see with endometriosis have low testosterone and low progesterone, and synthetic hormone treatments can lower these levels even further. Nicola now takes estradiol, progesterone and testosterone and told me she feels the best she has since she was 12, which shows how much women with endometriosis can gain when they are offered the right hormones.

A man would never have both testicles removed and be sent home without testosterone. So why is it still happening to women?

Every day I speak to women who have had both their ovaries removed and were never told their body would suddenly stop making progesterone, estrogen and testosterone and they should be prescribed hormone treatments. 

After a hysterectomy, many women are only offered estrogen, as if that’s the only hormone their ovaries ever made. Which is wrong.

In the Framingham Heart Study, 3,086 adults had CT scans of their visceral fat (the fat packed around the organs). The ones carrying more of it had more heart disease and more cancer over the next 5 years, even after accounting for BMI (JACC, 2013). This isn't a vanity problem.

It also starts earlier than most women are told. In the SWAN Heart Study (Menopause, 2021), visceral fat measured by CT climbed 8.2 percent a year, beginning about 2 years before the final period. That's biology, and most clinics are still only checking your weight.

Here's the prescription I give every patient, and it's what I do myself. I lift 3 days a week and do cardio 5; a 2023 meta-analysis of randomized trials in postmenopausal women (Frontiers in Endocrinology) found that exercise lowered visceral fat, although the paper doesn't report how each trial measured it. I eat protein at every meal, and I use olive oil, nuts, and fatty fish in place of saturated fat. In the NutriAct trial (Nutrients, 2024), adults 50 to 80 ate a diet high in unsaturated fat and plant protein for a year, with no calorie target, and their visceral fat went down on MRI.

I get at least 25 grams of fiber a day: food first, with a supplement where there are gaps. In a 5-year study of adults with CT scans (Obesity, 2012), every 10 grams more soluble fiber in the diet was linked to visceral fat building up 3.7 percent more slowly.

I skip ultra-processed foods, and I don't drink heavily. In older adults, more ultra-processed food was linked to more abdominal fat on DXA (Clinical Nutrition, 2021), and heavy or binge drinking was linked to more fat in and around the organs on CT (Journal of the American Heart Association, 2023).
When a patient has done all of this and meets the criteria, I prescribe a GLP-1. That's a medical indication.

You deserve a clinician who measures more than your weight.

For years, we've talked about menopause as a collection of symptoms. Hot flashes, night sweats, sleep disturbances. But what about the changes happening throughout the body that we can't necessarily feel?
 
I recently shared a reel about a fascinating new study published in Nature Medicine, and I wanted to take a closer look at what it means for women's health. One of the most important questions this research raises is whether we're paying enough attention to the timing of menopause when we study women's health and aging.
 
We know that bone loss accelerates around menopause, and cardiovascular and metabolic risks change during midlife. But women reach menopause at different ages, and looking at chronological age alone may obscure important biological patterns. That matters because when something changes can be just as important as what changes.
 
Could a better understanding of these patterns eventually help us recognize risks earlier? Identify better opportunities for prevention? Understand why women of the same age can have very different health trajectories?
 
Those are questions researchers still need to answer. This study adds to a growing body of evidence that menopause needs to be considered when we study women's long-term health. Our final menstrual period is one moment in a much longer biological transition. Understanding that transition more fully could change how we approach women's health for decades to come.

Only about 1 in 10 menopausal women on Medicare uses vaginal estrogen, even though it cuts recurrent UTIs by more than half. That gap isn’t a patient failure; it’s the legacy of a boxed warning that sat on this drug for more than 20 years, built on data from a trial that never studied it.

Laura Trujillo lauratrujillowords at USA TODAY reported today that the FDA is exploring making some vaginal estrogen products available over the counter, possibly as soon as mid-2027. It isn’t approved yet: the FDA still needs evidence that women can use it safely without a clinician, and those studies are underway.

The data behind the push is striking. In a study of nearly 2 million women with recurrent UTIs, led by urologist Dr. Elise De, women 55 and older using vaginal estrogen were about half as likely to be hospitalized for a UTI, with sepsis and death rates roughly one-fifth as high. It’s observational, so it can’t prove cause, but it fits decades of consistent research.

Generic vaginal estradiol is approximately $13-$15 a tube. If insurance stops covering it, cost becomes the new barrier, and blood in your urine or infections that keep coming back still need a workup. You don’t have to wait for 2027. If you have recurrent UTIs, dryness, or pain with sex, ask your clinician about vaginal estrogen now.

More than 35 million American women over 50 have low bone mass or osteoporosis: 8.2 million with osteoporosis and another 27.3 million with low bone mass, according to NHANES data published in the Journal of Bone and Mineral Research in 2014. Half of women over 50 will break a bone from osteoporosis. And the test that finds it isn’t reaching them.
In a study of more than 1.6 million privately insured women published in the American Journal of Medicine in 2017, only 26.5 percent of women 65 to 79 had a DXA scan in a two-year window; for women 80 and older, it was 12.8 percent. Among women who went on to break a hip, only 20.1 percent had been screened in the two years before (Archives of Osteoporosis, 2022). Of the women who were screened, 86.6 percent had osteopenia or osteoporosis on their report. Ten percent were treated.
It isn’t only women over 65. Among menopausal women aged 45 to 64 who broke a wrist, about 1 in 8 had a bone density test within a year, and the average wait was 4.7 months (Injury, 2025). A broken wrist in your 50s is a bone health event; it gets a cast and nothing else.

Women deserve a plan before the hip fracture, not after. What you can do is in the comments.

I am at the International Menopause Society Meeting and heard a great research presentation yesterday. I write all the details for TheVajenda.com

The PAMELA trial is a 26-week randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial. The treatment arm is a female-specific testosterone product was dosed to the premenopausal range.

The primary aim was to determine the effect of physiologic-dose testosterone versus placebo on lower-limb muscle power using two-leg vertical jump mechanography.

The secondary aims were to determine the effects of testosterone versus placebo on muscle mass, muscle strength, neuromuscular quickness, dynamic balance, and static balance.

A total of 146 women completed the study, and there was no difference in the primary outcome between testosterone and placebo. 

Of the 5 secondary outcome measures, two had some minor changes that favored testosterone, but the magnitude of change was very small and so the clinical significance is unknown. 

The authors concluded the study provides limited support for physiologic-dose testosterone as a strategy to improve muscle mass and function for relatively healthy, active postmenopausal women.

“How long should I stay on HRT?” is a question I get all the time. Many women worry if it’s even worth starting if they might have to stop soon after.

The truth is, there’s no “hard and fast” rule that you must stop after five years. It’s a very individual decision based on your own health.

Here is what we consider:

👉 Individual Assessment: We regularly weigh up if the benefits of staying on HRT outweigh any risks for you personally.

👉 Modern Safety: Using newer, body-identical HRT is a much safer option.

👉 Protective Benefits: When started during perimenopause or early menopause, HRT protects your bones and likely your heart and blood vessels too.

👉 Feeling Better: Most importantly, it helps you feel like yourself again.

The best approach is to have regular chats with your doctor to stay up to date with the latest guidance and ensure the best outcome for you.

What if the story you’re telling yourself about menopause is quietly shaping how you experience it?

“I’m getting old.”

“I’ve let myself go.”

“My body doesn’t work anymore.”

“Maybe this is just who I am now.”

Here’s what I want you to understand.

Your brain is not a passive observer of your life.

Your expectations influence what you pay attention to, how you interpret experiences, and what you remember.

Psychologists call some of these processes selective attention and confirmation bias.

And when you’ve spent years telling yourself you’re failing, it’s easy to turn every disappointing weigh-in, missed workout or difficult day into another piece of evidence against yourself.

While overlooking the progress you’re making.

But this goes so much deeper than your weight.

What happens when you start believing menopause is the beginning of your decline?

That your energy will never return.

That you’re not as capable as you used to be.

That your best years are behind you.

You may start lowering your expectations.

Stop pursuing the things you want.

Stop believing you can feel phenomenal again.

And that’s the part I want to challenge.

Because your hormonal changes are REAL.

Your symptoms are REAL.

And none of this means you can simply think your way out of perimenopause.

But your beliefs can influence how you respond to what you’re experiencing.

And that’s something you can begin to change.

Start noticing what’s working.

Look for evidence of the promises you’re keeping.

Approach setbacks with curiosity instead of self-criticism.

And stop treating every difficult moment as proof that you’re failing.

Menopause is not the beginning of the end.

You have an extraordinary amount of life left to live.

And I want you going ALL IN on who you’re becoming.

Not someday.

NOW.

Before your feet hit the floor in the morning, gently wake up your joints.

Joints feel stiff in the morning because they’ve had relatively little movement overnight. Joint fluid distribution,  surrounding tissues and underlying conditions like osteoarthritis, inflammatory arthritis or menopause can all contribute.

Gentle movement can restore mobility, warm up the muscles and reduce the feeling of stiffness.

Video sped up. Move slowly and mindfully: 
1) Spread the fingers and rotate hands and feet five times in one direction and five times in the other direction

2) hug one knee to chest and hold for five breaths then hug the other knee

3) Placing feet wider than hips, drop both of knees  to one side then to the other side. 

4) Give yourself a full body stretch by reaching with the heels in one direction and the fingertips in the other

5) slowly make your way to a comfortable seated position and twist to one side stay there for five breaths then twist to the other side

6) seated cat cows mobilise the spine. Place your hands on your knees, inhale to lift the chest and look up at the ceiling then exhale rounding the spine and bringing your chin towards your chest 5 times.

In my last newsletter, I wrote about perimenopause and menopause hormone therapy: how to spot the signs of perimenopause, how to find the right healthcare provider, and what to expect when you start MHT. Today, I’m picking up where I left off with the part I feel most strongly about: what active women should know and consider about MHT.

MHT is a tool, and a good one, but—as with so many things—lifestyle can be just as powerful (if not more so for some) and needs to be considered too. 

As I mentioned in Part 1, most experts now use the term MHT rather than HRT, because the goal isn’t to “replace” the hormones you once had. That distinction is the root of a lot of confusion.

The hormones in MHT don’t behave exactly like the ones your ovaries made. Treatment doses aim for a steady, low physiological level, not the higher pulses and rhythms of your natural cycle, and your body responds differently to them. So replacing some estrogen doesn’t mean restoring everything estrogen once did. 

How you take estradiol matters:

- Pills (oral) are processed by the liver before reaching the rest of the body, so much of the estradiol is converted to estrone, a weaker estrogen. The liver also makes more clotting proteins, which slightly raises the risk of blood clots. 

- Patches and gels (transdermal) absorb through the skin straight into the bloodstream, keeping a more natural balance of estrogens with little effect on the liver. 

MHT can ease menopausal symptoms and protect tissues like bone and the vaginal and urinary tract, but it isn’t a like-for-like replacement.

That’s why the research shows MHT is first and foremost a tool for symptom relief, with bone protection as its clearest long-term benefit. The literature doesn’t show it builds muscle, drives fat loss, or prevents heart disease (one major trial suggests it may slow early arterial changes when started soon after menopause, but that’s not the same as prevention). This is where the lifestyle levers like sleep, exercise, and nutrition really come to the fore.

Lifting weights is now recognized as good for more than “just” making muscle.

For decades, aerobic exercise was regarded as the primary form of exercise you should do for cardiovascular and other health benefits. Heck, that’s why endurance type exercise such as walking, biking, and running are commonly referred to as “cardio.” The physical activity guidelines have traditionally emphasized aerobic exercise for health, even though researchers have been talking about resistance training being good for your heart for more than twenty years.

“Resistance training not only can improve or maintain muscle mass and strength, but also has favorable physiological and clinical effects on cardiovascular disease and risk factors.” American Heart Association

Now, finally, the new American Heart Association (AHA) scientific statement in Circulation makes the argument that, “Resistance training not only can improve or maintain muscle mass and strength, but also has favorable physiological and clinical effects on cardiovascular disease and risk factors.”

The statement is an update from 2007, and summarizes the benefits of resistance training alone or in combination with aerobic training to improve traditional and non-traditional cardiovascular disease risk factors, especially since resistance exercise may be as effective as aerobic exercise for the prevention of chronic disease and improving health and lifespan.

Menopause hormone therapy (MHT) is one of the topics I’m asked about most, and the conversation around it has changed dramatically over the years. For two decades after the 2002 Women’s Health Initiative (WHI) study, women were told hormones were dangerous (which was largely a fault of media misinterpreting the design and results of the study). Now the pendulum has swung hard the other way, and if you believe everything you read on the internet you’d think every woman needs MHT, for life, or her health will fall apart.

The truth sits somewhere in the middle. MHT is a genuinely useful tool, and for many women it can be life-changing. But it isn’t a cure-all, and it doesn’t replace the lifestyle foundations that drive your health through midlife and beyond.

There’s so much to cover on this topic that I’ve split it into two parts. This week, we’ll cover recognizing the signs, finding the right provider, testing, and what to expect when you start. In my next newsletter on November 2, we’ll cover what MHT does (and doesn’t do) for your body, the testosterone question, non-hormonal options, and how long to stay on it.

An important note before we dive in: MHT is often also referred to as HRT (hormone replacement therapy) or simply HT (hormone therapy). They all describe the same treatment, but most experts now prefer MHT, because the goal isn’t to "replace" the hormones you previously had. It’s to ease symptoms and protect your health through this stage of life.

I’ve also asked my friend Dr. Kiki Silver to weigh in on some of the practical, in-clinic questions, since I am not a medical doctor. We spend a lot of time talking about muscle, metabolism, and performance, but not nearly enough time talking about the brain. Yet women are disproportionately affected by cognitive decline and Alzheimer’s disease. Alzheimer’s is a brain condition that slowly damages memory, thinking, learning, and organizational skills. It is an abnormal buildup of amyloid and tau proteins that prevent neurons from working as they should.

There is not enough attention drawn to the fact that nearly two-thirds of Alzheimer’s cases are women, and women have a greater lifetime risk of developing the disease than men (the risk is 1 in 5 for women versus 1 in 10 for men). Women are often diagnosed later than men because the key memory tests doctors use rely on verbal skills—and women tend to do better on those, even in the early stages of decline. As a result, problems can be missed at first. But once symptoms do show up, women often decline more quickly, likely because they have a higher buildup of harmful tau proteins in the brain. This may be linked to differences in how women’s brains naturally clear out damaged cells and waste.

Although there is clearly a knowledge gap (as there is with so much of the health and fitness data women rely on), we can begin tracing the answers back to female biology, hormones, and how our brains respond to stress, inflammation, and aging across the lifespan. Let’s examine these factors more closely.

That approach needs to account for the specific vulnerabilities of your history, address the physiological realities of being a woman in perimenopause or post-menopause, and keep you strong, fast, and capable for decades. Women respond differently to resistance training than men. We’re generally more fatigue-resistant, recover faster between sets, and often tolerate higher total training volumes. At the same time, gains in muscle mass can be slower, particularly if we're under-fueling, due to differences in muscle fiber behavior and anabolic signaling.

Hormones matter, but not in the rigid way they’re sometimes presented online.

Estrogen supports muscle repair, collagen synthesis, and neuromuscular coordination, which helps explain why some women may feel stronger or more powerful at certain times during their cycle. It also helps explain why we see a precipitous drop in power with an increase in soft tissue issues during perimenopause. However, responses are highly individual. Rather than prescribing training strictly by menstrual cycle phase (as we once used to), current best practice is to use individual symptoms, recovery, and performance feedback to guide when to push and when to pull back. Fixed calendar rules aren't supported by the evidence—and they're not how most women actually experience training.

For peri- and postmenopausal women, declining estrogen makes resistance training even more important for maintaining muscle quality, strength, and bone density. One of the questions I’m often asked is: How connected are building muscle and building strength?

The short answer: they’re related, but not the same. You can increase strength without dramatically increasing muscle, and you can increase muscle without seeing proportional gains in strength. Strength: 3–5 reps
Size: 6–12 reps
Endurance: 15+ reps
